prompt: A seating chart numbers seats 0 to 99, and you jump straight to seat 42 to check who sits there.
why: Seats are numbered positions, so the program jumps straight to slot 42 without looking at the others. Reaching an item by its number is what an array does.
trap: A map could work, but the keys are just positions.

prompt: A game stores the high score for each day of the week, Monday as 0 through Sunday as 6.
why: Each day is a fixed number from 0 to 6, and the score sits at that number. A small set of numbered slots is an array.
trap: The days are numbered positions, not keys to hash.

prompt: An image is a grid of pixels, and the program reads the color at row 10, column 20 directly.
why: Row and column are two numbers that pick one cell directly. A grid you index by position is a two-dimensional array.
trap: Neighbouring pixels aren't a graph you walk; you jump by position.

prompt: A playlist keeps songs in order, and the app shows song number 5 the moment you tap it.
tells: song number 5 the moment you tap it
why: The app can show song 5 at once because it computes where item 5 is instead of walking to it. Instant access by position is an array's strength.
trap: A linked list would have to walk to song 5.

prompt: Inserting a name at the front of a long list is slow because every other name has to shift one place.
tells: every other name has to shift one place
why: Arrays keep items side by side in memory, so inserting at the front pushes every later item along one place. That shifting cost is the giveaway.
trap: A linked list avoids the shifting; the slow list described is an array.

prompt: Temperatures are logged every hour into slots numbered 0 to 23.
why: Each hour has its own numbered slot, and the reading goes into that slot. Storing by position number is an array.
trap: Nothing is waiting in line; it's storage by position.
